---
title: Defining Your Project's People
---

*“Coming together is a beginning, staying together is progress, and working together is success”.* Henry Ford

For your project to succeed, you need to think carefully about who needs to be involved, what they bring to the project, and how they can participate. There are two groups to think about: the volunteers who will make up your internal team and the external stakeholders.

## Start With Your Internal Team

One of the strengths of the projects at Civic Tech DC is that we can bring together folks with very different skills and experiences. Yes, software engineers and developers are important, but so are designers, organizers, researchers, and policy experts who can complement each other with their strengths. 

For example, while a developer might build the tool, a designer helps understand what users actually need. There are many times when a tool is built, but when brought to the community for feedback, the developers learn the community doesn’t need it or find it useful. Having multiple perspectives means you can approach the same problem holistically from multiple angles.

## Expand to the Stakeholders 

Your internal team will only see part of the problem, and sometimes, after you've been with a project for a long time, it becomes harder to identify assumptions. Civic Tech DC projects benefit from bringing in people who experience the problem or experts in the domain area of your problem. This is different from your community partner (see here). 

Your external network might include a journalist who can highlight your work in a blog or a researcher who has spent years covering an issue and can help you understand the broader landscape. It's important to note that while this group of stakeholders starts to develop later in the project (once they can see what you are building and how they can help), having a list of potential stakeholders in mind helps. 

The important question is not simply “Who can use our product?” It is:

> “Who can help us understand this problem better and make the project more useful?”

### Create Different Pathways for Participation

Not everyone you talk to needs to become a formal project partner. In fact, asking every person for a large commitment \can make it harder to build relationships.

Instead, create different levels of participation depending on what someone can offer and what you need from them.

Someone might participate in a one-time interview to help you understand the problem. Someone else might become an advisor who you check in with periodically. A community organization might become a design or research partner, helping you recruit users and test ideas. A government office might eventually become an implementation partner that integrates the tool into its work. Another organization might simply become a champion, helping introduce the project to people who could benefit from it.

This also creates more opportunities for people on your internal team. A newer team member might start by conducting interviews, then take ownership of user research, while a more experienced member builds the external relationship. Someone interested in policy could start by researching the issue and eventually become the team's policy lead.

Think of partnership as a pathway rather than a binary decision. Someone does not have to say “yes, I will partner with your project” before you can learn from them.
